title: Before the Domain Name System (DNS), the internet’s entire address book was one text file
body: Every web address you type is looked up through the Domain Name System, but the ARPANET, the internet’s predecessor, had no such system. The Stanford Research Institute kept a single text file, **HOSTS.TXT**, mapping every computer’s name to its numerical address, and shared it with member sites. To add a machine, you contacted Elizabeth Feinler’s Network Information Center by telephone during business hours. By the early 1980s the method had become slow and unwieldy, and in 1983 Paul Mockapetris created the Domain Name System, which spreads the job across a tree of domains instead.

slides.heading: Joining the network, 1970s style
items: Phone the Network Information Center at the Stanford Research Institute, in business hours
Your computer’s name and address go into HOSTS.TXT
Member sites pick up the updated file by file sharing

slides.prompt: Elizabeth Feinler, who ran the Network Information Center, and her team came up with something you type every day. What?
slides.answer: Domains: her team developed the concept, such as edu for universities
slides.detail: Feinler suggested basing domains on where a computer physically was, so educational institutions would get edu.

slides.heading: From one file to a system

events.text: Request for Comments (RFC) 226 lists host names
Feinler’s team run the naming registry

slides.heading: How DNS finds an address today

steps.label: A root server points it to the org servers
They point to Wikipedia’s own name servers
Those reply with the address; it gets cached

slides.question: Why did a single HOSTS.TXT file stop working in the early 1980s?
options: It got slow and unwieldy as hosts grew
A virus deleted the master copy
slides.explanation: One central table had to be updated and redistributed for every change. DNS automated publication and let each domain manage its own names.
